I finally found an explanation that caused my jaw to drop. Code is speculatively executed, and can read from kernel, but it can't write result because exception occurs. But, it can still affect what's in the cache, effectively leaving data behind. Attack code gets 256 pages of data in cache, speculatively executes code which reads a kernel byte, then accesses an array such that each byte value evicts a different one of the original 256 pages from the cache. Then attack code finds which page was evicted by timing accesses to the pages, finding the one that takes longer than the others. Attack code has now read a byte from the kernel.

This is really bad.

EDIT: The Spectre ones are worse, because they can violate boundaries even in software, e.g. array bounds in a virtual machine:

At a high level, a Spectre attack violates memory isolation boundaries by combining speculative execution with data exfiltration via microarchitectural covert channels. More specifically, in order to mount a Spectre attack, an attacker starts by locating a sequence of instructions within the process address space which when executed acts as a covert channel transmitter which leaks the victim’s memory or register contents. The attacker then tricks the CPU into speculatively and erroneously executing this instruction sequence, thereby leaking the victim’s information over the covert channel. Finally, the attacker retrieves the victim’s information over the covert channel. While the changes to the nominal CPU state resulting from this erroneous speculative execution are eventually reverted, changes to other microarchitectural parts of the CPU (such as cache contents) can survive nominal state reversion.

An example:

if (x < array1_size) y = array2[array1[x] * 256];

This will leak what value was read from array1[x] via the cache, even if x is out of bounds but the code is speculatively executed. So the sandboxed code could read the whole process space.
